newsitem.title: INDONESIA: East Timor war of words spills into cyberspace.
newsitem.headline: East Timor war of words spills into cyberspace.

text.p: For a small island in a remote corner of the world, East Timor has a prominent place on the Internet.
There is an ever growing on-line free-for-all where anybody can have an opinion and their version of the facts on the vexed questions surrounding the former Portuguese colony.
Never before have so many had such an easy way of accessing facts, figures, disinformation and propaganda on the disputed territory.

Whether it is the views of those who still resist Indonesian rule after its 1975 invasion and annexation the following year, or the position of the Indonesian government in developing what it calls its 27th province, information abounds.
ONLINE COUNTER-ATTACK
But now Indonesia's military (ABRI) has given an indication it feels it is losing the war of words in cyberspace about what it refers to as its "integration" of the territory.
"In this matter, there is not yet one vision or similar perception," ABRI spokesman Brigadier-General Slamet Supriadi said recently in a classic understatement.

Jakarta-appointed East Timor Governor Abilio Soares launched a homepage (http://www.dfa-deplu.go.id/timtim/) on the 21st anniversary of the annexation of East Timor on July 18 in an effort to counter foreign information about East Timor on the Internet.
"The information (on the Internet) does not match the facts in the field. Much of the news on the Internet is engineered by the foreign press," Soares was quoted as saying by the Kompas daily.
"The regional government, through the Internet, will ward off bad rumours about Indonesia by showing the facts which are experienced by the community," he said.
LATE START

A simple search engine query for "East Timor" shows the Internet has been a battleground for many years and, unlike the activists, Indonesia has failed to grasp the power of the medium and has much ground to regain in the war of words and images.
An Alta Vista search on East Timor throws up around 5,000 sites, many privately run by people around the world who oppose Jakarta's 1975 occupation of the territory just north of Australia.

ABRI's own site (www.mil.id), on the web since 1995 but still only in Indonesian rather the web's lingua franca English, gives a lengthy justification of Indonesia's involvement in East Timor seemingly aimed at local rather than foreign audiences.

It refers to the joint forces of a number of small East Timor political parties "taking" the Timor capital Dili on December 7, 1975, with the help of Indonesian "volunteers", but makes no reference to the 20,000 ABRI regulars which foreign intelligence agencies estimated took part in the invasion that month.
DIFFERENT PICTURE

On the United Nations web site (www.un.org) documents can be found showing the world body does not recognise Indonesia's subsequent 1976 annexation of East Timor, and it still regards Portugal as being the administering power.
The U.N. website contains extensive records of the meeting last June of the body's decolonisation committee which discussed at length the problems in the territory since the 1975 invasion.

Institutions such as the International Committee of the Red Cross (www.icrc.org) and human rights watchdog Amnesty International (www.amnesty.org) have been watching events closely in East Timor over the past 22 years too.

East Timor was pushed to the forefront of the world's attention again last year with the awarding of the Nobel Peace Prize (www.nobel.se) in October to two East Timorese, neither of whom is considered an ally of ABRI.
Since then, coverage of events in the territory on mailing lists and abundant homepages have abounded, often skewed against Jakarta's position.

But while these days East Timor is no longer on the world's front pages after the burst publicity when Catholic Bishop Carlos Belo and pro-independence activist Jose Ramos Horta won their Nobel prizes, the territory's status is still a hot Internet issue.
SCENES OF TORTURE ON DISPLAY

"Without doubt I believe you'll see the Internet becoming more important to the Timorese as a weapon in the information war," Hugh Ekeberg, an activist who runs one of the graphic East Timor torture photograph sites, told Reuters.

Ekeberg's site (http://dayworld.net.au/ekeberg/torture.html) is one of two sites operated by Australian-based, pro-independence activists showing pictures purportedly of Indonesian soldiers torturing East Timorese resisting Jakarta's rule.

The Melbourne-based East Timor Human Rights Centre (www.peg.apc.org/etchrmel), with its own extensive site on East Timor, has a different set of pictures allegedly showing Indonesian security force personnel torturing Timorese.

The long-time defender overseas of ABRI's sometimes brutal domestic policies, Indonesia's foreign affairs department (www.dfa-deplu.go.id) has hit back on its English site with "The Untold Story of East Timor".
The department says the pictures are fakes. Analysts say their authenticity is difficult to verify.

"The people who would be influenced by the photographs would be those who already have a position on East Timor and are anti-Indonesian," an Indonesian foreign affairs official, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.
"I don't think the impact of Internet can yet be compared to print media and television, but we can't ignore it," he said.
